name: Sensor and Shipping Data
title: Sensor and Shipping Data
answer: Sensor and shipping data is a category of alternative data built from physical measurements and logistics records. It includes vessel positions from AIS, port calls, container movements, rail and truck telemetry, warehouse scans, weather sensors, and industrial IoT readings. Analysts use it to estimate trade flows, inventory levels, freight activity, and supply chain stress before official statistics appear. It overlaps with satellite imagery, customs records, and bill of lading data, but its defining feature is that the signal comes from machines or transport operations rather than from company disclosures. For The AI Economist, it is one input into a broader picture of economic activity and AI-related markets.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Sensor and shipping data is a category of alternative data built from physical measurements and logistics records. It includes vessel positions from AIS, port calls, container movements, rail and truck telemetry, warehouse scans, weather sensors, and industrial IoT readings. Analysts use it to estimate trade flows, inventory levels, freight activity, and supply chain stress before official statistics appear. It overlaps with satellite imagery, customs records, and bill of lading data, but its defining feature is that the signal comes from machines or transport operations rather than from company disclosures. For The AI Economist, it is one input into a broader picture of economic activity and AI-related markets.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The data runs on networks of sensors, transponders, and telemetry systems. AIS transponders on ships, GPS receivers on trucks, RFID and barcode scanners in warehouses, port community systems, and satellite constellations feed raw events into collection pipelines. Those pipelines depend on message brokers, time-series databases, cloud storage, and geospatial indexes to handle high volume and location data. Downstream, analysts query the data through APIs, dashboards, or data warehouses, often joining it with reference tables for vessels, ports, and companies.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Work begins with ingestion and cleaning, because sensor feeds arrive with gaps, duplicates, and clock errors. Teams normalize vessel and port identifiers, map coordinates to known locations, and build voyage or shipment episodes from raw pings. They then compute features such as port congestion, transit time, draft change, or container dwell time, and compare those features against benchmarks or historical patterns. Statistical models and machine learning can fill gaps, detect anomalies, or forecast activity, but the core task is careful entity resolution and validation against independent sources. Results are usually delivered as time series, indices, or exception alerts rather than as raw pings.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk depend on where the data comes from and what contracts allow. AIS is broadcast publicly, but some feeds are aggregated by commercial providers with terms that restrict redistribution, and vessel owners may object to tracking that reveals commercial activity. Shipping records can include personal data about crews or counterparties, so privacy and data protection rules may apply, and customs or bill of lading data may be subject to confidentiality. Provenance matters because AIS can be spoofed, disabled, or delayed, and port data can be revised, so common practice includes documenting sources, retaining raw evidence, and flagging uncertainty. Governance also covers access controls, retention limits, and audit trails for any model or index built on the data.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward denser sensor coverage, with more satellites, cheaper trackers, and broader port digitalization. That increases the resolution of trade and logistics signals but also raises the volume of noise and the cost of cleaning. Expect more fusion of shipping data with satellite imagery, weather, and customs records to cross-check physical flows. Regulation and commercial licensing will shape what can be shared, and provenance standards will matter as more models rely on these feeds. For analysts, the practical direction is toward faster nowcasts of supply chains and economic activity, with clearer documentation of where each number came from.
